citation.title: Institutional Accountability of Nonstate Actors in the UNFCCC: Exit, Voice, and Loyalty
citation.venue_or_publisher: Review of Policy Research (Policy Studies Organization)
citation.type: Publisher's version, early online (journal header on page 1 shows 'Volume 00, Number 00 (2016)'; file dated 2016-11-09, modified 2016-12-14)

question: How nonstate actors within the UNFCCC are held to account by one another; the authors introduce 'institutional accountability' (demands for justification through shared rules, norms and procedures, followed by sanction through exit, voice or loyalty).
data: Illustrative qualitative case study of the nine UNFCCC constituency groups. Sources: UNFCCC documents, event observations, constituency position papers, NGO websites, and more than 40 semi-structured interviews (Bonn 2013, COP19 Warsaw 2013, COP20 Lima 2014, Bonn 2015, with COP21 observation). Interviewees listed in the appendix. No participant-list data and no counts of delegates by sector.
method: Theory-building plus illustrative case examples from on-site observation and interviews; not a comprehensive inventory and not a test of each constituency. No classification of organisations, no coding, no language model use.

definitions.definition: Nonstate actors are formally divided into nine constituencies, one of which is business.
definitions.quote: This group of nonstate actors is formally divided into nine constituencies within the UNFCCC system including businesses, nongovernmental organizations (NGOs), trade unions, indigenous groups, and several more.

definitions.definition: Accredited observer groups are clustered into nine constituencies.
definitions.quote: These observer groups are clustered into nine constituencies with diverse but recognizable interests.

definitions.definition: The business constituency; with ENGO, one of the first two constituencies to organise. The paper gives no further definition of what counts as business.
definitions.quote: The first two constituency groups to organize within the UNFCCC system were the Business and Industry NGOs (BINGO) and the Environmental NGOs (ENGO).

definitions.definition: BINGO members range from pro-regulation companies to anti-regulatory and climate-sceptic ones.
definitions.quote: Its diverse membership ranges from green pro-regulatory coalitions of companies to anti-regulatory and even climate-skeptical members.

definitions.definition: Observers may list themselves with more than one constituency, but this is not common.
definitions.quote: Observer groups are allowed to list themselves

definitions.definition: Accountability arising from shared institutional rules, norms and procedures, with exit, voice and loyalty as sanctions.
definitions.quote: institutional frameworks provide a shared terrain of rules, norms, and procedures which are employed by agents (accountability wielders) to demand justification from other members

proxies.indicator: Membership of the BINGO constituency (business and industry organisations). The paper does not itself use this as a counting rule.
proxies.quote: The first two constituency groups to organize within the UNFCCC system were the Business and Industry NGOs (BINGO) and the Environmental NGOs (ENGO).

proxies.concept: Fossil fuel-linked business (as perceived by interviewees)
proxies.indicator: Qualitative split of BINGO into 'gray' anti-mitigation fossil-fuel companies and 'green' pro-regulation companies, taken from other researchers (Vormedal 2008; Yamin and Depledge 2004). No criteria, thresholds or company list.
proxies.quote: the BINGO constituency has from its inception been divided between “gray” anti-mitigation fossil-fuel companies and “green” pro-regulation companies.

proxies.concept: Business association positions on fossil fuels (interviewee view)
proxies.indicator: An interviewee places three business associations on a fossil-to-green scale: WBCSD (big fossil side), ICC (centrist), European Business Council for Sustainable Energy (green).
proxies.quote: the World Business Council of Sustainable Development (WBCSD) represents the big fossil side industry, the International Chamber of Commerce

proxies.concept: Fossil company influence inside a business association
proxies.indicator: A named oil company is described as a strong member of ICC, the body that holds the BINGO focal point.
proxies.quote: the ICC, who assigns the focal point for BINGOs, has Exxon-Mobil as a strong and influential member known for the most aggressive anti-climate stance among all oil companies.

findings.claim: COP21 Paris had almost 40,000 delegates, 25,000 of them governmental (citing a Carbon Brief analysis in footnote 13); the rest were civil society, UN agencies and media.
findings.quote: COP21 in Paris gathered almost 40,000 delegates, of which 25,000 were from governmental representatives

findings.claim: The introduction gives different COP21 figures (10,000 nonstate actors and nearly 35,000 state delegates). The two passages are not reconciled in the text.
findings.quote: 10,000 nonstate actors descended on Le Bourget conference center to attend the negotiations alongside nearly 35,000 state delegates.

findings.claim: Nonstate actors are said to be near numerical parity with government delegates, and delegations increasingly include nonstate actors. No figures or delegation breakdown are given here.
findings.quote: In this institutional context, nonstate actors are increasingly on numerical parity with government delegates, and delegations also progressively include more nonstate actors

findings.claim: More than 2,000 observer organisations were accredited at COP21.
findings.quote: At COP21 in Paris, more than 2,000 observer organizations were accredited and admitted.

findings.claim: The nine constituencies hold the large majority of admitted NGOs.
findings.quote: These nine constituency groups contain more than 90% of all NGOs admitted during each COP

findings.claim: Constituency members get some access benefits, including secondary badges when site access is limited.
findings.quote: Constituency members receive: access to the Plenary floor so as to make interventions, allocation of secondary badges when site access is limited, advance information from the Secretariat

findings.claim: The local government constituency (LGMA) pushes governments to include more local government representatives in national delegations. This is the only point in the paper about government delegation composition.
findings.quote: At the same time, the constituency is encouraging national governments to have more local government representatives on their delegations.

findings.claim: BINGO does not advocate on policy inside the UNFCCC, but its members lobby governments and delegations individually, for fossil fuels among other things.
findings.quote: Differences are manifest when individual BINGO members make use of formal and informal networks to lobby individual governments and delegations

findings.claim: BINGO is internally divided between fossil and green positions but presents a unified face, using closed-door meetings.
findings.quote: While it is clear that BINGO is divided between “green” and “brown” carbon emission reduction efforts, these views are rarely aired in public.

limitations.point: Interviewees from ENGO were reluctant to speak about the CAN-CJN split, which limits the evidence on that case.
limitations.quote: A methodological limitation facing analysis of CAN-CJN, however, is that virtually all of our interviewees from ENGO were reluctant to speak about the fractions between CAN and CJN.

limitations.point: The study is illustrative, not a full inventory; some constituencies (RINGO, Farmers, IPO) are not analysed.
limitations.quote: We do not provide a comprehensive inventory of all interactions between nonstate actors within the UNFCCC

limitations.point: Not about country delegations or Party badges. It gives no counts of business delegates, no sector scheme, no definition of fossil fuel-linked, no list of companies and no financial-exposure measure. Its data is from 2013 to 2015 and covers observer constituencies, not Party delegations. States' own accountability behaviour is set aside.
limitations.quote: As such, the ways in which states may engage in “institutional accountability” is bracketed from our analysis.

limitations.point: The paper describes the observation period inconsistently: three years in the abstract, four years later in the text.
limitations.quote: we draw upon four years of on-site observation at COPs and Intersessionals.

limitations.point: No instructions addressed to a reader or an AI were found in the text.
